'''2.''' In ''old law'', probably, food or sustenance for cattle which is yielded by bushes and trees.

'''bosch''', ''n.'' See ''bosh''<sup>4</sup>.

'''boschbok, boshbok''' (bosh′bok; D. pron. bosk′bok), ''n.'' [D. ''boschbok'', < ''bosch'', wood, = E. ''bush''<sup>1</sup>, + ''bok'' = E. ''buck''<sup>1</sup>.] A name given by the Dutch colonists to an antelope of the genus ''Tragelaphus'', as ''T. sylvaticus''. Also written ''bushbok''.

'''boschvark, boshvark''' (bosh′värk; D. pron. bosk′färk), ''n.'' [D. ''boschvark'', < ''bosch'', wood, = E. ''bush''<sup>1</sup>, + ''vark'', used only in dim. ''varken'', hog, = E. ''farrow'', q. v.] The name given by the Dutch colonists to the African bush-hog, bush-pig, river-pig, or guinea-pig, as the species of aquatic swine of the genus ''Potamochœrus'' are variously called. {{smaller|''P. africanus'', or ''P. pictus'', is a middle-sized swine with large, strong, protrusive canine teeth and penciled ears.}}

'''Boselaphus''' (bos-el′a-fus), ''n.'' [NL., irreg. < L. ''bos'' (Gr. βοῦς), ox (or rather NL. ''Bos'' as a generic name), + Gr. ἔλαφος, stag.] A genus of large bubaline antelopes, including the nylghau (''B. tragocamelus''), etc.

'''bosh'''<sup>1</sup>† (bosh), ''n.'' [Prob. < F. ''ébauche'' (cf. ''debosh'' and ''debauch''), a sketch, < OF. *''esboche'' = Sp. ''esbozo'' = Pg. ''esboço'' = It. ''sbozzo'' (also, with different prefix, ''abbozzo''), a sketch; with verb, F. ''ébaucher'', < OF. ''esbaucher'', ''esbocher'' = Pg. ''esboçar'' = It. ''sbozzare'' (also ''abbozzare'', sketch), < prefix ''s-'', ''es-'', L. ''ex-'', out, + ''bozza'', a rough draft, a blotch, swelling, = F. ''bosse'', > E. ''boss''<sup>1</sup>, q. v. Cf. OD. ''boetse'', ''bootse'', a sketch, D. ''boetseren'', mold, emboss, of same ult. origin.] A rough sketch; an outline; a figure.

{{smaller block|The ''bosh'' of an argument, . . . the shadow of a syllogism.
{{right|''The Student'', II. 287.}}}}

'''To cut a bosh''', {{smaller|to make a display; cut a figure.}}

'''bosh'''<sup>1</sup>† (bosh), ''v. i.'' [< ''bosh''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.''] To cut a figure; make a show. ''Tatler.''

'''bosh'''<sup>2</sup> (bosh), ''n.'' [< Turk. ''bosh'', empty, vain, useless, futile, void of meaning: a word adopted into E. use from Morier’s novel “Ayesha” (1834), in which it frequently occurs in its Turk. sense: as, “this firman is ''bosh''—nothing.”] Utter nonsense; absurd or foolish talk or opinions; stuff; trash. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|This is what Turks and Englishmen call ''bosh''.
{{right|''W. H. Russell.''}}
I always like to read old Darwin’s Loves of the Plants, ''bosh'' as it is in a scientific point of view.
{{right|''Kingsley'', Two Years Ago, x.}}}}

'''bosh'''<sup>2</sup> (bosh), ''v. t.'' [< ''bosh''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.''] To make bosh or nonsense of; treat as bosh; spoil; humbug. [Slang.]

'''bosh'''<sup>3</sup> (bosh), ''n.'' [See ''boshes.''] '''1.''' See ''boshes.'' —'''2.''' A trough in which bloomery tools (or, in copper-smelting, hot ingots) are cooled. ''Raymond'', Mining Glossary.

'''bosh'''<sup>4</sup>, '''bosch''' (bosh), ''n.'' [Short for ''Bosch butter'', i. e., imitation butter made at ''’s Hertogenbosch'' or ''den Bosch'' (F. ''Bois-le-Duc''), lit. ‘the duke’s wood,’ a city of the Netherlands: D. ''bosch'' = E. ''bush''<sup>1</sup>.] A kind of imitation butter; butterine: a trade-name in England.

'''boshah''' (bosh′ä), ''n.'' [Turk.] A silk handkerchief made in Turkey.
readings.c1s3:
¶
'''boshes''' (bosh′ez), ''n. pl.'' [Cf. G. ''böschung'', a slope, < ''böschen'', slope, < G. dial. (Swiss) ''bösch'', turf, sod.] The lower part of a blast-furnace, extending from the widest part to the top of the hearth. {{smaller|In the older forms of blast-furnace there was a marked division into specific zones. In many of the more approved modern forms there are no such definite limits, but a gradual curvature from top to bottom. In such cases it is difficult to say where the boshes begin or end.}}

'''Bosjesman''' (bosh′ez-ma̤n), ''n.'' [S. African D.] Same as ''bushman'', 2.

'''bosk''' (bosk), ''n.'' [< ME. ''boske'', also ''buske'', unassibilated forms of ''bush''<sup>1</sup>, q. v. Cf. ''boscage'', ''bosky''.] A thicket; a small close natural wood, especially of bushes. [Old and poetical.]
{{smaller block|Blowing ''bosks'' of wilderness. ''Tennyson'', Princess, i.
<poem>The wondrous elm that seemed
To my young fancy like an airy ''bosk'',
Poised by a single stem upon the earth.</poem>
{{right|''J. G. Holland'', Kathrina, i.}}}}

'''boskage''', ''n.'' See ''boscage''.

'''bosket, bosquet''' (bos′ket), ''n.'' [< F. ''bosquet'' (= Sp. ''bosquete'' = It. ''boschetto''), dim. of OF. ''bos'', a thicket: see ''bois'', ''bosk'', ''bush''<sup>1</sup>, and cf. ''bouquet'' and ''boscage''.] A grove; a thicket or small plantation in a garden, park, etc., formed of trees, shrubs, or tall plants. Also written ''busket''.

'''boskiness''' (bos′ki-nes), ''n.'' [< ''bosky'' + ''-ness''.] The quality of being bosky, or covered with thickets.

'''Boskoi''' (bos′koi), ''n. pl.'' [Gr. βοσκοί, pl. of βοσκός, a herdsman, < βόσκειν, feed, graze.] An ancient body of monks in Palestine and Meso-

'''bosky''' (bos′ki), ''a.'' [< ''bosk'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''busky'', ''bushy''.] Woody; consisting of or covered with bushes; full of thickets.
{{smaller block|This is Britain: a little island with little lakes, little rivers, quiet ''bosky'' fields, but mighty interests and power that reach round the world. ''The Century'', XXVII. 102.
<poem>
In lowliest depths of ''bosky'' dells
The hermit Contemplation dwells.
</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', Questions of Life.}}}}

{{right|''Fortnightly Rev.'', N. S., XXXIX. 146.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' A native or an inhabitant of Bosnia.

The hermit Contemplation dwells.

{{smaller block|All this petty persecution has made Austrian rule odious among the ''Bosniacs.''
{{right|''Fortnightly Rev.'', N. S., XXXIX. 146.}}}}

'''Bosnian''' (bos′ni-an), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< ''Bosnia'' + ''-an.'']   '''I.''' ''a.'' Of or pertaining to Bosnia, a nominal province of Turkey, lying west of Servia, the administration of which was transferred to Austria-Hungary by the Berlin Congress of 1878.

'''II.''' ''n.'' A native or an inhabitant of Bosnia.

'''bosom''' (bu̇z′um or bö′zum), ''n.'' and ''a.''   [Early mod. E. also ''bosome'', ''boosome''; < ME. ''bosom'', ''bosum'', ''bosem'', < AS. ''bōsum'', ''bōsm'' (= OS. ''bōsom'' = OFries. ''bōsm'' = D. ''boezem'' = MLG. ''busem'', ''bōsem'', ''bossen'', LG. ''bussem'' = OHG. ''buosum'', ''buosam'', MHG. ''buosem'', ''buosen'', G. ''busen''), bosom; perhaps orig., like ''fathom'', the space between the two arms; with formative ''-sm'', < ''bōh'', ''bōg'', arm: see ''bough''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' The breast; the subclavian and mammary regions of the thorax of a human being; the upper part of the chest.
{{smaller block|And she turn’d—her ''bosom'' shaken with a sudden storm of sighs.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Locksley Hall.}}}}
'''2.''' That part of one’s clothing which covers the breast; especially, that portion of a shirt which covers the bosom, generally made of finer material than the rest.
{{smaller block|And he put his hand into his ''bosom'' again; and plucked it out of his ''bosom'', and, behold, it was turned again as his other flesh.
{{right|Ex. iv. 7.}}}}
'''3.''' The inclosure formed by the breast and the arms; hence, embrace; compass; inclosure: as, to lie in one’s ''bosom''.
{{smaller block|They which live within the ''bosom'' of that church.
{{right|''Hooker''.}}}}
{{smaller block|And it came to pass, that the beggar died, and was carried by the angels into Abraham’s ''bosom''.
{{right|Luke xvi. 22.}}}}
'''4.''' The breast as the supposed abode of tender affections, desires, and passions.
{{smaller block|Their soul was poured out into their mothers’ ''bosom''.
{{right|Lam. ii. 12.}}}}
{{smaller block|Anger resteth in the ''bosom'' of fools.
{{right|Eccl. vii. 9.}}}}
{{smaller block|Hence the weighing of motives must always be confined to the ''bosom'' of the individual.
{{right|''Jevons'', Polit. Econ., p. 16.}}}}
'''5†.''' Inclination; desire.
{{smaller block|You shall have your ''bosom'' on this wretch.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., iv. 3.}}}}
'''6.''' Something regarded as resembling or representing in some respect the human bosom as a sustaining surface, an inclosed place, the interior, the inmost recess, etc.: as, the ''bosom'' of the earth or of the deep. {{smaller block|Upon the ''bosom'' of the ground.{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, iv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Slips into the ''bosom'' of the lake.{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, vii.}}}}
'''7.''' A recess or shelving depression around the eye of a millstone.—{{smaller|'''In Abraham’s bosom,''' in the abode of the blessed: in allusion to the parable of Dives and Lazarus, Luke xvi. 19-31.—'''In the bosom of one’s family,''' in the privacy of one’s home, and in the enjoyment of family affection and confidence.—'''To take to one’s bosom,''' to marry.}}

'''II.''' ''a.'' [The noun used attributively.] Of or pertaining to the bosom, either literally or figuratively. {{smaller|In particular—(''a'') Worn or carried on or in the bosom: as, a ''bosom'' brooch. (''b'') Cherished in the bosom: as, a ''bosom'' sin; a ''bosom'' secret. (''c'') Intimate; familiar; confidential: as, a ''bosom'' friend.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I know you are his ''bosom''-counsellor.</poem>{{right|''Fletcher and Rowley'', Maid in the Mill, ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''bosome'' admonition of a Friend is a Presbytery and a Consistory to them.{{right|''Milton'', Ref. in Eng., i.}}}}

'''bosom''' (bu̇z′um or bö′zum), ''v. t.''   [< ''bosom'', ''n.'']   '''1.''' To inclose, harbor, or cherish in the bosom; embrace; keep with care; cherish intimately.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Bosom'' up my counsel,
You’ll find it wholesome.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Pull from the lion’s hug his ''bosom’d'' whelp.{{right|''J. Baillie.''}}}}
'''2.''' To conceal; hide from view; embosom.
{{smaller block|<poem>To happy convents, ''bosom’d'' deep in vines.</poem>{{right|''Pope'', Dunciad, iv. 301.}}}}

'''bosom-board''' (bu̇z′um-bōrd), ''n.'' A board upon which the bosom of a shirt or other garment is ironed.

'''bosomer''' (bu̇z′um-ėr or bö′zum-ėr), ''n.'' One who or that which embosoms. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Blue! ’Tis the life of heaven — the domain
Of Cynthia . . . the ''bosomer'' of clouds.</poem>
{{right|''Keats'', Sonnet.}}}}

'''bosom-spring''' (bu̇z′um-spring), ''n.'' A spring rising in the bosom or heart; heart-spring; heart-joy. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>From thee that ''bosom-spring'' of rapture flows
Which only Virtue, tranquil Virtue, knows.</poem>
{{right|''Rogers'', Pleasures of Memory, ii.}}}}

'''bosom-staff''' (bu̇z′um-stȧf), ''n.'' An instrument for testing the symmetry of the bosom or central concavity of a millstone.

'''bosomy''' (bu̇z′um-i or bö′zum-i), ''a.''   [< ''bosom'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   Full of sheltered recesses or hollows.   ''N. E. D.''

'''boson'''<sup>1</sup> (bō′sn), ''n.'' A corruption of ''boatswain'', representing its common pronunciation.
{{smaller block|<poem>The merry ''boson'' from his side
His whistle takes.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Albion and Albanius, ii. 3.}}}}

'''boson'''<sup>2</sup>†, ''n.''   [Appar. < OF. *''boçon'', dim. of ''boce'', a boss: see ''boss''<sup>1</sup>.]   A bolt for the crossbow, having a round knob at the end, with a small point projecting from it.

'''bosporian''' (bos-pō′ri-an), ''a.''   [< ''bosporus'' + ''-i-an''.]   Pertaining to a bosporus, particularly (with a capital) to the Thracian or the Cimmerian Bosporus, or to the Greek kingdom of Bosporus named from the latter (about 500 {{sc|b. c.}} to {{sc|a. d.}} 259).
{{smaller block|The Alans forced the ''Bosporian'' kings to pay them tribute, and exterminated the Taurians. {{right|''Tooke.''}}}}

'''bosporus''' (bos′pọ̄-rus), ''n.''   [L., sometimes in erroneous form ''bosphorus'', < Gr. βόσπορος, a name applied to several straits, for βοός πόρος, lit. ox’s ford (cf. E. ''Oxford'', < AS. ''Oxenaford'', oxen’s ford): βοός, gen. of βοῦς, an ox (see ''Bos''); πόρος, passage, ford (akin to E. ''ford'') (> E. ''pore''), < περᾶν, pass over, cross, = E. ''fare'', go: see ''fare'', ''pore''<sup>2</sup>.]   A strait or channel between two seas, or between a sea and a lake. {{smaller|More particularly applied as a proper name to the strait between the sea of Marmora and the Black Sea, formerly the Thracian Bosporus, and to the strait of Yenikale, or Cimmerian Bosporus, which connects the sea of Azov with the Black Sea.}}

'''bosquet''', ''n.'' See ''bosket''.

'''boss'''<sup>1</sup> (bos), ''n.''   [< ME. ''bos'', ''bose'', ''boce'', a boss, < OF. ''boce'', the boss of a buckler, a botch or boil, F. ''bosse'', boss, hump, swelling, = Pr. ''bossa'' = It. ''bozza'', a blotch, swelling (also OF. (Norm.) ''boche'', > ME. ''bocche'', E. ''botch''<sup>1</sup>, q. v.); prob. < OHG. ''bōzo'', a bundle (of flax), ''bōz'', a blow, < ''bōzan'', MHG. ''bōzen'', G. ''bossen'', strike, beat, = E. ''beat''<sup>1</sup>: see ''beat''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''emboss''.]   '''1.''' A protuberant part; a round, swelling process or excrescence on the body or upon some organ of an animal or plant. Hence —'''2†.''' (''a'') A hump or hunch on the back; a humpback. (''b'') A bulky animal. (''c'') A fat woman.
{{smaller block|Be she neuer so straight, thinke her croked. And wrest all parts of hir body to the worst, be she neuer so worthy. If shee be well sette, then call hir a ''Bosse'', if slender, a Hasill twygge.
{{right|''Lyly'', Euphues, Anat. of Wit, p. 115.}}}}
{{smaller block|Disdainful Turkess and unreverend ''boss !''
{{right|''Marlowe'', Tamburlaine, I., iii. 3.}}}}
'''3.''' A stud or knob. {{smaller|Specifically, a knob or protuberant ornament of silver, ivory, or other material, used on bridles, harness, the centers of ancient shields, etc., or affixed}} to any object. Bosses are placed at regular intervals on the sides of some book-covers, for the purpose of preserving the gilding or the leather of the cover from abrasion.

{{smaller block|He runneth . . . upon the thick ''bosses'' of his bucklers.
{{right|Job xv. 26.}}}}
{{smaller block|On the high altar is placed the Statue of the B. Virgin and our Saviour in white marble, which has a ''bosse'' in the girdle consisting of a very faire and rich sapphire, with divers other stones of price. {{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Oct. 4, 1641.}}}}
{{smaller block|A number of prominent crags and ''bosses'' of rock project beyond the general surface of the ground.
{{right|''Geikie'', Ice Age, p. 17.}}}}
